questions.stem: Trial 556589685: a 192 g sample of brass undergoes a phase change with specific latent heat 208 J per g; compute the heat transferred in kJ.

options.misconception: Divided mass by latent heat instead of multiplying
Correct application of the principle
Reported joules instead of converting to kilojoules
Used a factor of one hundred rather than one thousand

questions.explanation: During a phase change the temperature stays constant while energy goes into rearranging the structure, so Q equals mass times specific latent heat. Here 192 g times 208 J per g gives 39936 J, or 39.94 kJ after dividing by one thousand.
questions.hint: Q = m L, then convert joules to kilojoules.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Molar Heat Capacity principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: Trial 599459162: a 4.0 mol quantity of oxygen with molar heat capacity 68 J per mol K is heated by 56 K; find the heat supplied in kJ.

options.misconception: Used moles times temperature without the heat capacity
Correct application of the principle
Dropped the number of moles from the calculation
Left the answer in joules instead of kilojoules

questions.explanation: When heat capacity is given per mole, the heat required is Q equals n times Cm times delta T. Multiplying 4.0 mol by 68 J per mol K by 56 K and dividing by one thousand yields 15.23 kJ.
questions.hint: Q = n Cm delta T with Cm in J per mol K.

questions.stem: Trial 221400362: a 50 g sample of lead at 109 degrees Celsius is dropped into 161 g of water at 15 degrees Celsius; if the final temperature is 32 degrees Celsius, find the specific heat of the metal in J per g K.

options.misconception: Omitted the metal cooling range from the denominator
Correct application of the principle
Swapped the metal and water temperature changes
Ignored the mass of water in the balance

questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives heat lost by metal equals heat gained by water, so mm cm (Tim minus Tf) equals mw cw (Tf minus Tiw). Solving for cm with water at 4.184 J per g K gives 2.974 J per g K; the two temperature differences must be kept in their correct positions.
questions.hint: Set m_metal c_metal (Ti - Tf) = m_water c_water (Tf - Ti) and solve.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Isothermal Expansion Heat principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: Trial 223885727: an ideal gas of nitrogen with 2.6 mol expands isothermally at 351 K from 2.8 L to 10.9 L; how much heat must be supplied, in kJ?

options.misconception: Omitted the logarithm from the work expression
Correct application of the principle
Halved the temperature in the nRT factor
Altered the volume ratio by adding one to it

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy does not change, so by the first law the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas, nRT ln(Vf over Vi). With the given volumes and temperature this is 10.33 kJ; heat must flow in to balance the expansion work.
questions.hint: At constant T for an ideal gas, Q = W = nRT ln(Vf/Vi).

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Adiabatic Process principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: Trial 381562911: starting at 347 K, an ideal gas of argon with gamma 1.4 expands adiabatically from 2.3 L to 5.5 L; find the final temperature.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Inverted the initial-to-final volume ratio
Assumed temperature scales linearly with volume
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one as the exponent

questions.explanation: For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process T V raised to gamma minus one is constant, so Tf equals Ti times (Vi over Vf) to the power gamma minus one. With gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving a final temperature of 244.5 K; expansion cools the gas because it does work with no heat entering.
questions.hint: Use Tf = Ti (Vi/Vf)^(gamma - 1) for adiabatic expansion.

questions.stem: Trial 314861027: at a constant 248 kPa, a piston fitted with brass hardware expands a gas whose volume rises by 7.4 L; calculate the work done by the gas in joules.

options.misconception: Doubled the volume change before multiplying
Correct application of the principle
Assumed constant volume so that no work is done
Divided pressure by the volume change

questions.explanation: At constant pressure the work done by the gas is P delta V. With pressure 248 kPa and volume increase 7.4 L, and using one kPa litre equal to one joule, the work is 1835 J. A rigid constant-volume step would instead do zero work, but this process has a moving piston.
questions.hint: For isobaric expansion, W = P delta V.

questions.stem: Trial 523708701: at 526 K, compute the root-mean-square speed of a gas molecule whose molar mass is 0.0202 kg per mol, using R equal to 8.314 J per mol K.

options.misconception: Treated the molar mass as if it were in grams
Used the mean speed formula with 8RT over pi M
Used the most probable speed formula with 2RT over M
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: The root-mean-square speed follows from kinetic theory as v rms equals the square root of 3RT divided by molar mass in kilograms per mole. Substituting 526 K and 0.0202 kg per mol gives 806 m per s; the factor of three reflects the three translational degrees of freedom.
questions.hint: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) with M in kg/mol.

questions.stem: Trial 962188182: a cyclic device built with aluminum components takes in 763 J of heat per cycle and rejects 410 J to the cold reservoir; determine the net work delivered per cycle.

options.misconception: Reported the absorbed heat as the useful work
Added the absorbed and rejected heat instead of subtracting
Correct application of the principle
Reported the rejected heat as the useful work

questions.explanation: Because the device returns to its starting state each cycle, the change in internal energy over a full cycle is zero, so the net work output equals the net heat input Qh minus Qc. That gives 353 J per cycle; the rejected heat is not available as work.
questions.hint: Over a cycle, delta U = 0 so W_net = Q_in - Q_out.
